extracted.intended_audience: litigation counsel, in-house IP lawyers, and strategists evaluating or selecting jurisdictions for international patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for assessing jurisdictions and strategic considerations when selecting forums for international patent enforcement and litigation, comparing factors such as market, adjudication quality, remedies, timing, costs, and fees recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 1 – The Market
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the size, commercial importance, and R&D/manufacturing footprint of the market (e.g., GDP, per-capita spending, R&D percentage, production growth in relevant industries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use market metrics to assess commercial relevance and enforcement value: examples include Netherlands GDP and R&D spend figures; China’s rapid growth in manufacturing and patent filings (PCT filings data). Consider where products are made, sold, imported, or used—markets with higher production/sales may make enforcement more valuable or practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 2 – The Quality of Adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether courts are specialized, experienced, independent, and technically literate; whether courts follow established patent law approaches (e.g., EPO problem-solution), and whether decisions are predictable and well-reasoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider existence of specialized first-instance/appeal courts (The Hague; China’s IP courts), life-appointed independent judges, low perceived corruption, application of EPO case law (problem-solution approach), availability of technical advisors, acceptance of foreign experts and English-language proceedings. Also consider 'smart court' features (online filing, video hearings, digital evidence handling) that affect efficiency and predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 3 – Time to Trial and Final Relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate timelines for first-instance and appellate decisions, availability and speed of preliminary relief, and existence of accelerated procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Netherlands: accelerated regime (VRO) yields first-instance merits decision in ~12–18 months (may be longer due to backlog); preliminary inter partes relief typically hearing in 8–16 weeks and decision 2–4 weeks later; appeals de novo 12–18 months (can be accelerated to 3–6 months), Supreme Court 1.5–2 years (error of law review). China: invalidation ~4–6 months, first-instance infringement ~9–18 months, appeal ~6–9+ months; preliminary relief timelines vary. Also note practical delays from court workload and that pendency of parallel invalidity/opposition does not automatically stay infringement proceedings in many jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 4 – Likelihood of Prevailing on the Merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider jurisdictional merits-stage patterns, whether courts bifurcate validity/infringement, and empirical win rates and substantive patentability rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Netherlands: absence of bifurcation means patentee must win on both infringement and validity; historical patentee success ~35% overall, ~42% in preliminary injunctions, ~30% in merits; appeal sometimes more patentee-friendly. China: specialized IP courts and reforms have yielded relatively high foreign-party win rates in some courts (e.g., Beijing IP Court ~68% reported); also consider local patentability rules (e.g., methods of diagnosis/treatment not patentable in China; software patentable) and how courts treat EPO case law or foreign decisions as persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 5 – Availability of Effective Relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which remedies are available (preliminary/inter partes/ex parte injunctions, permanent injunctions, damages, recall/destruction, disclosure orders, cross-border relief, seizures, customs action) and limits/exceptions to relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Netherlands: inter partes preliminary relief usually available (hearing in 8–16 weeks); ex parte relief only in exceptional cases (prima facie valid title, prima facie infringement/threat, irreparable harm); injunctive relief as a rule available where patent valid and infringed but may be denied for disproportionality, contractual/legal obligations (e.g., SEP/FRAND), compelling societal interest, or abuse of rights; cross-border relief covering EP territory possible when Dutch defendants engage in cross-border activities (permanent cross-border relief may be stayed if invalidity defense raised); preliminary civil seizure/ex parte evidence seizure (saisie-contrefaçon) is available to secure evidence/products but is preservatory and requires initiation of proceedings within a set term. China: wide range of relief including preliminary injunctions (subject to statutory factors), monetary damages (Article 71 methods/statutory range), permanent injunctions (may be denied for public interest), customs seizure available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 6 – Cost of Litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess expected litigation costs, and how rules (e.g., absence of discovery) and case complexity/expert involvement affect fees and overall expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Netherlands: generally cost-effective in part due to no discovery; straightforward first-instance cases possibly under €100,000, complex cases up to ~€500,000; full appeal costs ~75% of first-instance; FRAND/third-party issues can increase costs. China: litigation often less costly than U.S. (no discovery), but evidence-gathering (investigators, notarization for foreign evidence) and pre-litigation expenses add costs. Recovery of such costs is at court discretion in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor 7 – Recovery of Fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate prospects of recovering legal costs/attorneys’ fees from the losing party and any statutory or judicial limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Netherlands: winning party entitled to 'reasonable and proportionate' legal costs subject to court caps based on case complexity (ranges from €10,000 for simple preliminary injunction cases up to €250,000 for highly complex merits proceedings), caps include legal and patent counsel fees but exclude disbursements (experts); orders enforceable notwithstanding appeal. China: courts may award reasonable expenses (attorney and court fees) if sufficient evidence presented; absence of discovery typically lowers costs to recover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery / Disclosure regime
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the jurisdiction permits broad documentary discovery, and what alternative procedures exist for accessing opponent-held evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Netherlands: no general discovery/disclosure obligation; evidence known to exist can be seized via ex parte evidence seizure; inter partes access proceedings may follow seizures; amount of evidence required depends on defendant’s level of contestation. China: no extensive documentary discovery; litigants often use investigation firms and may request court orders for evidence preservation/production; foreign evidence may require notarization; preservation measures and evidence-seeking are available but different in scope from U.S.-style discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dutch ex parte evidentiary seizure (saisie-contrefaçon) / Preliminary civil seizure
rubrics_metrics.description: A preservatory ex parte procedure allowing a claimant to have evidence/products seized or described by a bailiff, subject to location/accessibility in the Netherlands and subsequent initiation of proceedings within a set term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: request filed mentioning IP rights and reasons for suspected infringement; court decree typically in days; bailiff may enter premises, describe or seize products and store them; seizure is conservatory—claimant must initiate infringement proceedings within a set term or seizure becomes void and items returned; inter partes access to seized evidence requires subsequent proceedings. Seizures can assist litigants in other jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dutch cross-border relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of cross-border injunctive relief in both preliminary and permanent proceedings covering the territory of a European patent when defendants engage in cross-border activities or via presence of Dutch distributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-border relief can extend to foreign manufacturers/customers when Dutch defendants act across borders; but if a defendant raises an invalidity defense permanent cross-border relief may be unavailable or stayed (see Art. 24(4) Brussels recast). Preliminary cross-border injunctions are generally not affected by pending invalidity defenses. Examples include cases where mere presence of a Dutch distributor supported cross-border measures; courts have granted or accepted cross-border jurisdiction in specific recent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: China – Specialized IP courts, 'Smart court' and procedural modernization
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess China’s specialized IP courts, unified appeal structure, and digitalization initiatives that affect case management and evidence handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: China has specialized IP courts/tribunals (Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Hainan) and a nationwide unified appeal court in Beijing. Courts use technical advisors and have been building 'smart court' systems (online filing, online hearings, blockchain evidence storage). These features can shorten timelines and increase predictability, but practical effects vary by locality and case type.

rubrics_metrics.name: China – Choice of jurisdiction and forum-shopping considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs may choose the province/city where alleged infringing acts occurred, enabling strategic filing in favorable localities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigants typically commence in a familiar or favorable jurisdiction (place of business, reputation for fairness, or higher success rates). Strategic links (e.g., purchasing infringing product from local distributor) may be used to establish connection to targeted jurisdiction. Consider local track records and receptivity to foreign litigants when selecting city/province.

rubrics_metrics.name: China – Preliminary injunction requirements (factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a preliminary injunction in China claimants must satisfy statutory/practical factors examining factual/legal basis, irreparable harm, balance of harms, public interest, and other relevant considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts generally consider: (1) whether claimant’s request has factual ground and legal basis; (2) whether failure to take preservation measures will cause irreparable harm or enforcement difficulty; (3) whether harm from not taking measures exceeds harm to defendant from measures; (4) whether injunction would prejudice public interest; and (5) other factors. Preliminary injunctive relief historically difficult in some patent matters due to risk of later invalidity, though courts are more willing in design patent cases where infringement is easier to determine.

rubrics_metrics.name: China – Damages framework and statutory remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand available monetary remedies, methods for calculating damages, statutory ranges, and enhanced/punitive damages for willful infringement under Chinese Patent Law (Article 71 and amendments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages may be assessed based on: (i) patentee’s actual losses; (ii) infringer’s profits; (iii) reasonably multiplied royalties; or (iv) statutory-type damages (RMB 30,000 to RMB 5,000,000 as example range). Recent amendments increased statutory damages and permitted punitive damages up to five times for willful infringement. Empirical data show an increasing proportion of higher-value awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customs / border detention measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability and practical use of customs detention/seizure measures to stop infringing goods entering or moving through the jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rights-holders can file border detention requests listing relevant IP rights and sufficient identifying details. Customs may retain matching goods and notify the IP proprietor, who can then inspect or initiate civil proceedings. Netherlands customs are noted as capable and active; China also provides customs seizure and detention orders as an enforcement tool. Use of customs can complement litigation and apply commercial pressure on alleged infringers.
